# Define API gateway routes on virtual machines

This topic describes how to configure HTTP and TCP routes and attach them to Consul API gateway listeners. Routes are rule-based configurations that allow external clients to send requests to services in the mesh.

## Overview

The following steps describe the general workflow for defining and deploying routes:

1. Define routes in an HTTP or TCP configuration entry. The configuration entry includes rules for routing requests, target services in the mesh for the traffic, and the name of the gateway to attach to.
1. Deploy the configuration entry to create the routes and attach them to the gateway.

Routes and the gateways they are attached to are eventually-consistent objects. They provide feedback about their current state through a series of status conditions. As a result, you must manually check the route status to determine if the route is bound to the gateway successfully.

## Requirements

The following requirements must be satisfied to use API gateways on VMs:

- Consul 1.15 or later
- A Consul cluster with service mesh enabled. Refer to [`connect`](/consul/docs/reference/agent/configuration-file/service-mesh#connect)
- Network connectivity between the machine deploying the API Gateway and a Consul cluster agent or server

### ACL requirements

If ACLs are enabled, you must present a token with the following permissions to
configure Consul and deploy API gateway routes:

- `mesh: read`
- `mesh: write`

Refer [Mesh Rules](/consul/docs/security/acl/acl-rules#mesh-rules) for
additional information about configuring policies that enable you to interact
with Consul API gateway configurations.

## Define the routes

Define route configurations and bind them to listeners configured on the gateway so that Consul can route incoming requests to services in the mesh.

1. Create a route configuration entry file and specify the following settings:
   - `Kind`: Set to `http` or `tcp`.
   - `Name`:  Specify a name for the route. The name is metadata that you can use to reference the configuration when performing Consul operations.
   - `Parents`: Specifies a list of API gateways that the route binds to.
   - `Rules`: If you are configuring HTTP routes, define a list of routing rules for constructing a routing table that maps listeners to services. Each member of the list is a map that may containing the following fields:
      - `Filters`
      - `Matches`
      - `Services`

   Refer to the [HTTP route configuration entry](/consul/docs/reference/config-entry/http-route) and [TCP route configuration entry](/consul/docs/reference/config-entry/tcp-route) reference for details about configuring routes.

1. Configure any additional fields necessary for your use case, such as the namespace or admin partition.
1. Save the configuration.


The following example routes requests from the listener on the API gateway at port `8443` to services in Consul based on the path of the request. When an incoming request starts at path `/`, Consul forwards 90 percent of the requests to the `ui` service and 10 percent to `experimental-ui`. Consul also forwards requests starting with `/api` to `api`.

```hcl
Kind = "http-route"
Name = "my-http-route"

// Rules define how requests will be routed
Rules = [
  // Send all requests to UI services with 10% going to the "experimental" UI
  {
    Matches = [
      {
        Path = {
          Match = "prefix"
          Value = "/"
        }
      }
    ]
    Services = [
      {
        Name = "ui"
        Weight = 90
      },
      {
        Name = "experimental-ui"
        Weight = 10
      }
    ]
  },
  // Send all requests that start with the path `/api` to the API service
  {
    Matches = [
      {
        Path = {
          Match = "prefix"
          Value = "/api"
        }
      }
    ]
    Services = [
      {
        Name = "api"
      }
    ]
  }
]

Parents = [
  {
    Kind = "api-gateway"
    Name = "my-gateway"
    SectionName = "my-http-listener"
  }
]
```

### Route to service subsets

When an `http-route` sends traffic to a single backend service, Consul API Gateway also evaluates the backend service's discovery chain. When the backend service has a `service-router` that routes matching requests to a `service-resolver` subset, the API gateway preserves that subset routing when it builds the gateway discovery chain.

You can expose an HTTP route at the gateway while using Consul service mesh traffic management, such as routing a subset of requests to a canary service version. Consul applies the `http-route` match and the `service-router` match. For example, a request must match the gateway route and the service-router rule before Consul routes it to the subset destination.

The following example routes requests with the `x-version: canary` header to the `canary` subset of the `api` service. All other requests that match the route use the `stable` default subset.

```hcl
Kind          = "service-resolver"
Name          = "api"
DefaultSubset = "stable"
Subsets = {
  stable = {
    Filter = "Service.Meta.version == stable"
  }
  canary = {
    Filter = "Service.Meta.version == canary"
  }
}
```

```hcl
Kind = "service-router"
Name = "api"
Routes = [
  {
    Match {
      HTTP {
        Header = [
          {
            Name  = "x-version"
            Exact = "canary"
          },
        ]
      }
    }

    Destination {
      Service       = "api"
      ServiceSubset = "canary"
    }
  },
]
```

```hcl
Kind = "http-route"
Name = "api-route"

Rules = [
  {
    Matches = [
      {
        Path = {
          Match = "prefix"
          Value = "/api"
        }
      }
    ]
    Services = [
      {
        Name = "api"
      }
    ]
  }
]

Parents = [
  {
    Kind        = "api-gateway"
    Name        = "my-gateway"
    SectionName = "my-http-listener"
  }
]
```

## TLS SDS service overrides

Route services can override listener/gateway default certificates by setting `TLS.SDS`.

### HTTP route service override

Use `Rules[].Services[].TLS.SDS` in `http-route`.

- `CertResource` is required when `SDS` is set.
- `ClusterName` is optional and inherited from effective listener/gateway SDS cluster when omitted.
- `Hostnames` must be set on the HTTP route when using service `TLS.SDS` overrides.

```hcl
Kind = "http-route"
Name = "api-route"

Parents = [
  {
    Kind = "api-gateway"
    Name = "my-gateway"
    SectionName = "my-http-listener"
  }
]

Hostnames = ["foo.example.com", "bar.example.com"]

Rules = [
  {
    Services = [
      {
        Name = "svc-foo"
        TLS = {
          SDS = {
            CertResource = "foo.example.com"
          }
        }
      },
      {
        Name = "svc-bar"
      }
    ]
  }
]
```

### TCP route service override

Use `Services[].TLS.SDS` in `tcp-route`.

- `CertResource` is required when `SDS` is set.
- `ClusterName` is optional and inherited from effective listener/gateway SDS cluster when omitted.
- TCP routes currently support at most one service.
- A TCP listener can only have one distinct effective TCP SDS override; conflicting overrides are rejected.

```hcl
Kind = "tcp-route"
Name = "my-tcp-route"

Parents = [
  {
    Kind = "api-gateway"
    Name = "my-gateway"
    SectionName = "my-tcp-listener"
  }
]

Services = [
  {
    Name = "payments"
    TLS = {
      SDS = {
        CertResource = "payments.internal.example.com"
      }
    }
  }
]
```

### Effective precedence

Certificate selection precedence is:

1. Route service `TLS.SDS`
1. Listener `TLS.SDS`
1. Gateway top-level `TLS.SDS`

## Configure passive health checks for routed services

Passive health checks configure Envoy outlier detection on the API gateway. When an instance of a routed service returns consecutive errors, the gateway removes the instance from its load balancing pool for a period of time and sends requests to the remaining healthy instances.

Passive health checks require Consul v2.1 or later. You can configure passive health checks in the following locations:

- Gateway-wide default: [`Defaults.PassiveHealthCheck`](/consul/docs/reference/config-entry/api-gateway#defaults-passivehealthcheck) in the `api-gateway` configuration entry. The default applies to every service that routes attached to the gateway target.
- Service-level override: `Limits.PassiveHealthCheck` on a destination service in an [`http-route`](/consul/docs/reference/config-entry/http-route#rules-services-limits-passivehealthcheck) or [`tcp-route`](/consul/docs/reference/config-entry/tcp-route#services-limits-passivehealthcheck) configuration entry.

When you configure both, the service-level passive health check replaces the gateway default for that service. Consul does not merge individual fields. When multiple routes on the same gateway target the same service, configure the same passive health check on each route because Consul applies only one of them to the service.

### Define a gateway-wide default

The following example configures a default passive health check on the `api-gateway` gateway:

```hcl
Kind = "api-gateway"
Name = "api-gateway"

Listeners = [
  {
    Name     = "listener-one"
    Port     = 9999
    Protocol = "http"
  }
]

Defaults = {
  PassiveHealthCheck = {
    Interval                = "10s"
    MaxFailures             = 3
    EnforcingConsecutive5xx = 80
    MaxEjectionPercent      = 25
    BaseEjectionTime        = "30s"
  }
}
```

### Override the default for a service

The following example routes `/s1` requests to the `s1` service, which inherits the gateway default, and routes `/s2` requests to the `s2` service, which uses its own passive health check:

```hcl
Kind = "http-route"
Name = "api-gateway-route"

Parents = [
  {
    Kind        = "api-gateway"
    Name        = "api-gateway"
    SectionName = "listener-one"
  }
]

Rules = [
  {
    Matches = [
      {
        Path = {
          Match = "prefix"
          Value = "/s1"
        }
      }
    ]
    Services = [
      {
        Name = "s1"
      }
    ]
  },
  {
    Matches = [
      {
        Path = {
          Match = "prefix"
          Value = "/s2"
        }
      }
    ]
    Services = [
      {
        Name = "s2"
        Limits = {
          PassiveHealthCheck = {
            Interval                = "20s"
            MaxFailures             = 5
            EnforcingConsecutive5xx = 60
            MaxEjectionPercent      = 50
            BaseEjectionTime        = "60s"
          }
        }
      }
    ]
  }
]
```

You can configure upstream circuit-breaker limits, such as `MaxConnections`, in the same `Defaults` and `Limits` blocks. Unlike passive health checks, Consul applies service-level circuit-breaker limits field by field, and inherits any unset limit from the gateway default.

### Verify the passive health check

Complete the following steps to verify that the gateway applies the passive health check:

1. Read the configuration entries to confirm that Consul stored the passive health check settings:

   ```shell-session
   $ consul config read -kind api-gateway -name api-gateway
   $ consul config read -kind http-route -name api-gateway-route
   ```

1. On the machine that runs the API gateway, query the Envoy admin interface for the outlier detection configuration of the `s2` cluster. By default, the Envoy admin interface listens on `localhost:19000`.

   ```shell-session
   $ curl --silent localhost:19000/config_dump \
       | jq '.configs[]
         | select(."@type" | contains("ClustersConfigDump"))
         | .dynamic_active_clusters[]
         | select(.cluster.name | startswith("s2."))
         | .cluster.outlier_detection'
   ```

   The output contains the values from the route's passive health check:

   ```json
   {
     "consecutive_5xx": 5,
     "interval": "20s",
     "base_ejection_time": "60s",
     "max_ejection_percent": 50,
     "enforcing_consecutive_5xx": 60
   }
   ```

   Run the same command for the `s1` cluster to verify that it uses the gateway default values.

## Route requests with inverted header matches

Set `Invert` to `true` on a header match in an `http-route` to negate the condition. Inverted header matches let you route requests when a header is absent or when a header value does not equal a specific value. For example, you can send requests without a canary header to a stable service and requests with the header to a canary service.

Inverted header matches require Consul v2.1 or later. Refer to [`Rules[].Matches[].Headers[].Invert`](/consul/docs/reference/config-entry/http-route#rules-matches-headers-invert) in the HTTP route configuration reference for how `Invert` affects each match type.

The following example routes requests that do not include the `x-canary` header to the `s2` service, and routes requests that include the header to the `s1` service:

```hcl
Kind = "http-route"
Name = "canary-route"

Parents = [
  {
    Kind        = "api-gateway"
    Name        = "api-gateway"
    SectionName = "listener-one"
  }
]

Rules = [
  {
    Matches = [
      {
        Headers = [
          {
            Name   = "x-canary"
            Match  = "present"
            Invert = true
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
    Services = [
      {
        Name = "s2"
      }
    ]
  },
  {
    Matches = [
      {
        Headers = [
          {
            Name  = "x-canary"
            Match = "present"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
    Services = [
      {
        Name = "s1"
      }
    ]
  }
]
```

The following example routes requests to the `service-v2` service when the `x-version` header is present and its value is not `v1`:

```hcl
Kind = "http-route"
Name = "version-route"

Parents = [
  {
    Kind        = "api-gateway"
    Name        = "api-gateway"
    SectionName = "listener-one"
  }
]

Rules = [
  {
    Matches = [
      {
        Headers = [
          {
            Name   = "x-version"
            Match  = "exact"
            Value  = "v1"
            Invert = true
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
    Services = [
      {
        Name = "service-v2"
      }
    ]
  }
]
```

For `exact`, `prefix`, `suffix`, and `regex` matches, an inverted condition does not match requests that do not include the header. To match requests that do not include a header, use the `present` match type with `Invert = true`.

### Verify inverted header matches

Complete the following steps to verify that the gateway applies the inverted header match:

1. Read the route configuration entry and confirm that the header match includes `"Invert": true`. Confirm that the route status shows that the route is bound to the gateway.

   ```shell-session
   $ consul config read -kind http-route -name canary-route
   ```

1. On the machine that runs the API gateway, query the Envoy admin interface for the route configuration. By default, the Envoy admin interface listens on `localhost:19000`. The header matcher for the inverted condition includes `"invert_match": true`.

   ```shell-session
   $ curl --silent localhost:19000/config_dump \
       | jq '.configs[]
         | select(."@type" | contains("RoutesConfigDump"))
         | .dynamic_route_configs[].route_config.virtual_hosts[].routes[].match.headers'
   ```

1. Send requests with and without the header. Replace `GATEWAY_ADDRESS` with the address of the API gateway listener. The first request routes to the `s2` service, and the second request routes to the `s1` service.

   ```shell-session
   $ curl http://GATEWAY_ADDRESS:9999/
   $ curl --header "x-canary: true" http://GATEWAY_ADDRESS:9999/
   ```

## Deploy the route configuration

Run the `consul config write` command to attach the routes to the specified gateways. The following example writes a configuration called `my-http-route.hcl`:

```shell-session
$ consul config write my-http-route.hcl
```
